# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

# Review: "Two Years On" — Varden 24-Month Follow-up and Halden Subset

This is a strong follow-up. It does what the earlier exchange called for:
- a second, stricter hours measure (system logs);
- a registered mediation test;
- pre-period calendar data on meetings;
- difference-in-differences comparison of counter waiting times against control offices;
- a direct test of persistence within a controlled study.

Its headline conclusions are well supported. The case-processing per-hour gain declined but persisted. Both earlier extreme positions ("entirely an artifact" and "no sign of decay") are refuted.

The weaker points:
- the summary compares numbers measured on different hours bases;
- the mediation result is stated more strongly than one trial reusing its own offices allows;
- control-office contamination is reported but not followed through;
- the meetings pathway is probably partly accounting rather than behaviour, and the paper should say so.

## Arithmetic check

| Claim | Check |
|---|---|
| Per hour, timesheets, 24 months: +9.8% | 0.966 / 0.88 = 1.098 ✓ |
| Per hour, logs, 24 months: +8.5% | 0.966 / 0.89 = 1.085 ✓ |
| Mediation shares | 47 + 18 + 35 = 100 ✓ |
| Halden continuers: hours −13.4% | 34.9 / 40.3 = 0.866 ✓ |
| Halden continuers: +11.8% per hour | 96.8 / 86.6 = 1.118 ✓ |
| Counter cost +9% from 12% more staff | Consistent only if wages are about 75% of cost per contact. State the assumption. |
| **Control meeting time 7.2 → 7.0** | **Hard to square with two control offices cutting from 7.1 to 5.0; see §3** |

## 1. The summary compares across hours measures

The summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months." The 12.5% uses timesheets and the 8.5% uses system logs. The like-for-like comparison is 12.5% → 9.8%, a decline of about 22%, not about 32%.

The body handles this correctly ("on the like-for-like timesheet measure"). The summary should do the same, for example: "12.5% → 9.8% on timesheets; 8.5% on the stricter log measure."

Section 5's "declined by about a quarter" is closer to the timesheet comparison. It should name which measure it means.

There is also no formal test of the decline itself. The 9-month and 24-month CIs overlap heavily (+6.9 to +18.4 against +4.6 to +15.2). "Consistent with some fading" is fair. "The gain has declined" as a finding needs a test of the change, or a softer wording.

## 2. The mediation result is stated too strongly

**It is a pre-registered test on the same offices, not a replication.** The hypothesis came from the 7 treated case-processing offices at month 6. The registered test runs on the same 7 offices (plus controls), and the 24-month outcome window may include months 1–9. Registering at month 11 does prevent the model being tuned to the 24-month outcomes, which is worth having. But "survives a registered test" claims more than a confirmatory test on data the hypothesis was derived from can show.

**The effective sample is 14 clusters.** "A larger sample of office-months" does not add independent information. Office-months within an office are correlated, and the treatment varies only between the 14 offices. A CI of 28–66% for an indirect-effect share estimated from 14 clusters looks narrow. State how the CI was computed, and whether a cluster bootstrap or similar small-sample method was used.

**Two mediators, two assumptions.** The pathway shares are additive only if the mediators don't interact and aren't causally linked. Fewer meetings plausibly *reduce* fatigue, which would move credit between the two pathways. Report the mediator correlation, or a sensitivity analysis with fatigue placed downstream of meetings.

**The no-unmeasured-confounding assumption deserves concrete examples.** The obvious confounder is manager quality. Managers who cut meetings may also manage case flow better. The limitations name the assumption but not this example.

## 3. Part of the meetings pathway may be accounting, not behaviour

Whether system log time includes meeting time decides how to read the mediation result, and the paper doesn't say.

**If logs include meetings,** then moving hours out of meetings and into casework raises output per total hour automatically, with no change in how fast anyone works. A back-of-envelope version, using the nine-month baseline of about 37.9 hours and assuming control hours stayed stable:
- treated non-meeting time at 24 months ≈ 33.4 − 3.9 ≈ 29.5 hours;
- control non-meeting time ≈ 37.9 − 7.0 ≈ 30.9 hours;
- so non-meeting time is about 4.5% lower in treated offices;
- against an output-per-FTE difference of −3.4%, output per non-meeting hour is roughly flat.

On that rough calculation, meeting reduction accounts for nearly all of the per-hour gain, not 47%.

**If logs exclude meetings** (pure casework time), the log fall of 11% is hard to reconcile with meetings falling by 3.5 hours inside a total that fell about 4.5 hours.

Either way:
- state what the log measure includes;
- reconcile the mediation estimate with this accounting check;
- say plainly whether the meetings pathway means people work faster or simply that less of their time goes to meetings.

Both are real gains for the employer, but they mean different things for whether the gain could be had without cutting hours.

## 4. Two control offices cut meetings, and the paper doesn't follow this through

The "unplanned observation" is that two control offices cut meetings in month 15. That makes it a contamination problem for the comparison:

- **The decline may be partly the control group catching up.** If control offices improved their output per hour, the treated-minus-control gap shrinks even if treated offices held steady. Report treated and control trajectories separately from month 9 to month 24. That shows whether the decline is fading in treated offices or improvement in control offices. The two support very different conclusions about novelty.
- **The control meeting averages don't obviously add up.** Two of seven control offices fell by about 2.1 hours each. If the other five were unchanged, the control mean should fall by about 0.6 hours, but the reported change is −0.2. Either meetings in the other control offices rose, or the two offices' cuts partly reversed by month 24. Reconcile this.
- **The 4.1% gain in those two offices** compares them with their own previous six months. It is not adjusted for seasonality or for trend in the other control offices. "Suggests, without establishing" is the right hedge.
- **A sensitivity analysis is needed.** Report the 24-month estimates with these two offices excluded, alongside the full intention-to-treat estimate.

## 5. Halden subset

- **Who responded matters.** Fourteen of 23 organisations responded. The nine non-responders may disproportionately include organisations that reverted or struggled. The "upper bound" framing is right; non-response deserves to be stated next to it.
- **"Client-facing or coverage obligations" stretches to cover a marketing agency.** A marketing agency with client deadlines is nominally discretionary work in the meta-analysis's terms. Its reversion suggests the discretionary/coverage line is not clean: external deadlines can act like coverage requirements. The meta-analysis flagged this limit, and this case is evidence for it. Say so rather than folding it into "client-facing."
- **The 11.8% includes no reverters.** The three that reverted had output of 88–91 at reversion. A figure covering all 14, or one that bounds the reverters' effect, would help readers.
- **Correcting the record on Halden attrition.** Varga & Holm showed that the original Halden working paper misdescribed when and why nine organisations withdrew. With a Halden author (Okafor) co-authoring this follow-up, the report should acknowledge that correction explicitly. Section 5 credits the re-analysis on measurement but is silent on attrition.

## 6. How it engages the earlier papers

- **On Varga & Holm.** The rebuttal of "entirely an artifact" is sound. The Varden 24-month design meets every standard that paper set out. But the observed decline (about 22% on timesheets) partly supports their *direction* of argument, even though it refutes their magnitude. The report's "right about the measurement problems… not supported that nothing remains" is fair. It could add that they were also right that some fading occurs.
- **On the meta-analysis.** Showing that all four long-follow-up studies were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours confirms the suspected flaw directly and decisively.
- **On "not consistent with falling to zero by month ten."** Varga & Holm extrapolated self-reported *energy* in *Halden*, not output in Varden. The rebuttal stands, but it should be stated as rebutting an inference rather than a prediction about Varden.

## Smaller points

- **Small-cluster inference.** With 7 offices per arm, the earlier concern about clustered standard errors still applies. State the method behind the 24-month CIs. "Excludes zero by a clear margin" (lower bound +3.4%) may narrow under a wild cluster bootstrap or randomisation inference.
- **Sick days.** The −27% still doesn't address whether a shorter schedule mechanically reduces sick days, by leaving fewer scheduled days on which to be absent. Report sickness per scheduled day.
- **Resignations.** 4.1% vs 7.9% is still a comparison of levels, not a difference-in-differences estimate, and gives no event counts.
- **Pre-period meeting data.** The nine-month report said meeting data were collected in month 6 only. Explain where the baseline figures (7.4 and 7.2) came from, presumably retrospective calendar extraction, and whether they are measured the same way as the month-24 figures.
- **Counter arm.** The waiting-time comparison against control (7.3 vs 4.0 minutes) is an improvement on the nine-month report. Its CI, and the cost-per-contact assumption, should be given.

## Bottom line

The key findings are credible:
- in case-processing work, a per-hour gain of roughly 8.5–10% persists at two years under randomised, record-based, log-measured conditions, with output per employee slightly below control;
- in coverage-bound work, the scheme failed on service and cost and was ended.

This is the most informative study in the set.

Before strong mechanistic claims are made, the mediation result needs:
- a clear statement of what log hours include;
- reconciliation with the simple meeting-time accounting;
- separate treated and control trajectories, given the control-office meeting audits;
- small-cluster inference.

The summary should compare like with like on hours measures.

Across all five documents, the evidence now points the same way. Per-hour gains in discretionary work are real but well below headline pilot figures, and fade somewhat over time. A large share of the gain appears to come from removing low-value time, especially meetings. Coverage-bound work loses output and service quality. That leaves one question open: could reorganisation alone, without cutting hours, deliver most of the gain? Only a trial with a reorganisation-only arm can answer it.
